name: Orthoceras
fact: A straight-shelled relative of today’s nautilus and squid. Like the nautilus, it rose and sank by changing the gas and water in the chambers of its shell. The polished “Orthoceras” stones sold today are mostly its later relatives, from Morocco.

name: Eurypterid (Sea Scorpion)
fact: Sea scorpions: hunters of shallow seas and lagoons, and the closest big relatives of spiders and scorpions. The largest, from the Devonian, grew longer than a person. Some may have crawled briefly onto land.

name: Jawless Fish (Agnathan)
fact: Among the earliest vertebrates — animals with backbones, like us. They had no jaws, just a simple mouth for taking in small food, and many wore armour of bony plates. Jaws came later, and our own line runs back through fish like these.

name: Cameroceras
size: Several metres (claims of 9 m cannot be checked)
fact: A giant straight-shelled cephalopod, a relative of today’s nautilus and squid, and one of the biggest animals of the Ordovician seas. Old claims of 9-metre shells come from broken pieces and cannot be checked; the longest complete shells of its relatives are about 3.5 m. Its whole line died out.

name: Conodonts
fact: Tiny eel-like animals known for more than a century only from their tooth-like parts — so common in rocks that geologists use them to tell the age of a layer. Whole bodies found in Scotland in the 1980s, with eyes, muscle blocks and a tail fin, showed they were early vertebrates.

name: Arandaspis
fact: One of the oldest fish known from more than scraps: a jawless fish with a bony head shield, from the sandstones of central Australia. How it fed is not known; it may have taken small food from the sea floor.

name: Strophomena (Brachiopod)
fact: A lamp shell: it looks like a clam but is not related to one. Brachiopods like Strophomena were among the commonest shelled animals of the Ordovician seas. A few hundred kinds live today, against many thousands known as fossils.

name: Didymograptus (Graptolite)
fact: Colonies of tiny filter feeders that drifted through Ordovician seas. Graptolites are so abundant in black shales that geologists use them as precise time markers. The name means written rock - their fossils look like pencil scratches on stone.

name: Streptelasma (Rugose Coral)
fact: A solitary horn coral: each one grew alone, like a little horn set in the sea floor, with a wrinkled outer wall — “rugose” means wrinkled. Rugose corals appeared in the Ordovician and lived until the end of the Permian.

name: Aegirocassis
fact: A giant, gentle relative of Anomalocaris that strained plankton with comb-like arms — the oldest giant filter-feeder known, playing the role of a whale.
know: Its fossils preserve two sets of side flaps, top and bottom. That helped show how those flaps became the double-branched legs of later arthropods.

name: Isotelus
fact: Ohio's state fossil. One specimen from Manitoba, Isotelus rex, is the largest complete trilobite ever found — longer than a child's arm.

name: Asaphus kowalewskii
fact: A trilobite with its eyes on stalks as tall as a periscope. It probably lay buried in mud with only its eyes above the surface.

name: Sacabambaspis
fact: An armoured jawless fish with its eyes set at the very front of its head, like headlights, and a permanently open mouth. It became an internet joke — and is one of the oldest well-preserved vertebrates.

name: Earliest land plants (spores)
fact: The first sign of plants on land is not a plant but its spores: tough little packets shed by moss-like plants that left no bodies.

name: Pentecopterus
fact: The oldest known sea scorpion, already as long as a person, named after an ancient Greek warship. Its fossils lie in a crater left by a meteorite impact.

name: Lunataspis
fact: The oldest known horseshoe crab. Its family has kept much the same shape for 445 million years.

name: Endoceras
size: Shell over 3.5 m; perhaps up to 6 m
fact: A straight-shelled relative of squid — possibly the largest animal of its age.
debate: The longest complete shell is 3.5 m. Claims of 6- to 9-metre giants come from broken pieces and old reports that cannot be checked.

name: Promissum
habitat: Cold sea beside an ice sheet
fact: A giant conodont, ten times bigger than most. Its fossils preserve eyes and muscle fibres, showing what these eel-like animals really were.

name: Astraspis
fact: An early jawless fish covered in armour studded with tiny star-shaped bumps — one of the oldest fishes known from more than scraps.

name: Sinoceras
fact: A squid relative in a long, straight, cone-shaped shell. Its fossils are so common in parts of China that the polished stone is sold as “pagoda stone”.
